# Course philosophy

Ecological modelling is not only a collection of statistical methods.
It is a way of thinking about ecological systems, observations, uncertainty
and evidence.

The main goal of this course is to develop statistical and computational
thinking necessary for understanding ecological data and building interpretable
models.

The course follows a generative perspective:

```
Ecological process
        ↓
Data generation
        ↓
Probability model
        ↓
Statistical model
        ↓
Inference and prediction
```

Students will learn not only how to fit models, but also how models can
generate data and how observations can be used to evaluate competing
explanations.

# Conceptual progression

The course follows the transition:

```
Ecological questions

        ↓

Data organisation and exploration

        ↓

Variation and probability distributions

        ↓

Data generation and simulation

        ↓

Likelihood and statistical inference

        ↓

Models of increasing complexity

        ↓

Uncertainty and prediction

        ↓

Bayesian hierarchical thinking
```

# Learning objectives

After completing the course, students should be able to:

- understand the philosophy of ecological models;
- organize and explore ecological datasets;
- identify different types of ecological variables;
- understand probability distributions as models of variation;
- simulate ecological data using R;
- explain the relationship between data and models;
- fit and interpret statistical models;
- quantify uncertainty;
- develop reproducible analyses using R and Quarto.

# Course structure

## Module 1: Introduction to ecological modelling

### Questions

- What is a model?
- Why do we need models in ecology?
- Description, explanation and prediction.

### Topics

- ecological hypotheses;
- conceptual models;
- statistical models;
- mechanistic versus statistical approaches;
- introduction to R, RStudio and Quarto.

---

## Module 2: Ecological data and variation

### Topics

- Types of ecological variables:

  - continuous;
  - discrete;
  - categorical.

- Structure of ecological datasets;
- Data organisation;
- Exploration and visualization.

---

## Module 3: Probability distributions and data generation

### Topics

- Random variation in ecological systems;
- Probability distributions as models of variation.

### Discrete distributions

- Bernoulli;
- Binomial;
- Poisson.

### Continuous distributions

- Normal;
- Gamma.

### Simulation

- Generating ecological datasets;
- Connecting processes and observations;
- Understanding model assumptions.

---

## Module 4: Likelihood and statistical inference

### Topics

- Parameters and estimates;
- Likelihood;
- Maximum likelihood estimation;
- Model comparison.

### Uncertainty

- Confidence intervals;
- Bootstrap approaches;
- Bayesian credible intervals.

---

## Module 5: Linear models

### Topics

- Response and predictor variables;
- Linear relationships;
- Model assumptions;
- Residuals;
- Interpretation.

---

## Module 6: Generalized linear models

### Topics

- Why linear models are not always appropriate;
- Link functions;
- Gaussian, Binomial and Poisson models.

---

## Module 7: Hierarchical ecological models

### Topics

- Structure of ecological datasets;
- Random effects;
- Mixed models;
- GLMMs.

---

## Module 8: Bayesian ecological modelling

### Topics

- Bayesian thinking;
- Prior information;
- Posterior distributions;
- Hierarchical Bayesian models.

---

## Module 9: Reproducible ecological research

### Topics

- R projects;
- Git and GitHub;
- Quarto;
- Data and code organisation;
- Reproducible workflows.

# Computational philosophy

Throughout the course, simulations will be used as a learning tool.

Students will explore:

- how ecological data can be generated;
- how statistical models recover underlying processes;
- how uncertainty arises;
- why different models lead to different interpretations.
